statement: Let $R>0$ and let $f$ be [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$, with values in a complex normed space, with finite order at every point. With $C_w(z)=\frac{R^2-\bar w z}{R(z-w)}$ there is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form and zero-free on $|z|<R$, such that $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ off a discrete set.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) on the closed disk $|z|\le R$.
The function $f$ is [locally nonzero](c:locally-nonzero-function) at every point of the closed disk, so its order is never $\infty$.

conclusion: There is a function $g$, meromorphic in normal form on the closed disk and zero-free on the open disk, with $f=\big(\prod_{|w|<R}C_w^{-\operatorname{ord}_w f}\big)\,g$ outside a discrete subset of the closed disk.

formal.difference: mathlib allows any real $R$ and treats $R\le 0$ as a trivial case with an empty open disk. Otherwise the statements agree.

proofs.name: Cancel by canonical factors
proofs.slogan: Multiply f by canonical factors that cancel its zeros and poles, then pass to the normal form.
proofs.scope: The case $R>0$. For $R\le 0$ the open disk is empty: take $g$ constant equal to $f(0)$ and the product empty.

roles.why: A positive radius makes the open disk nonempty and defines every canonical factor.
Meromorphy of $f$ gives a meromorphic product and only finitely many zeros and poles.
Finite order everywhere lets orders add, so the product has order $0$ at each point of the open disk.

steps.slogan: Show that each canonical factor has one simple pole and no zero.
steps.detail: Take $|w|<R$ and $|z|\le R$. Then $|R^2-\bar w z|\ge R^2-|w|R>0$, so $C_w$ has no zero on the closed disk. Its only [pole](c:pole-of-a-function) is $z=w$, and it is simple because the numerator is nonzero there. Hence $\operatorname{ord}_w C_w=-1$ and $\operatorname{ord}_z C_w=0$ for $z\ne w$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ has only finitely many zeros and poles in the open disk.
steps.detail: Near a point $p$ the function is $(z-p)^k h(z)$ with $h$ nonzero at $p$, because its order is finite. So the points with nonzero order have no accumulation point in the closed disk. A compact disk holds only finitely many of them, so $n(w)=\operatorname{ord}_w f$ is nonzero for finitely many $w$.

steps.slogan: Multiply $f$ by the finite product of the canonical factors raised to $n(w)$.
steps.detail: Put $\varphi=\big(\prod_w C_w^{n(w)}\big)f$, a finite product. At a point $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, the factor $C_w^{n(w)}$ has order $-n(w)$ and $f$ has order $n(w)$, so $\varphi$ has order $0$. At every other point of the open disk all factors have order $0$, so the order of $\varphi$ is that of $f$, which is $0$.

steps.slogan: Replace $\varphi$ by its meromorphic normal form $g$.
steps.detail: Changing $\varphi$ on a discrete set gives a function $g$ in normal form with the same orders at every point. At a point of the open disk the order is $0$, so $g$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) there and $g(z)\ne 0$. The set where $g\ne\varphi$ is discrete.

steps.slogan: Multiply back by the inverse product to recover $f$ off a discrete set.
steps.detail: Away from the finitely many $w$ with $n(w)\ne 0$, $C_w^{-n(w)}C_w^{n(w)}=1$ pointwise. Hence $f=\big(\prod_w C_w^{-n(w)}\big)\varphi$ there, and $\varphi=g$ off a discrete set. The excluded points form a discrete set, which gives the stated identity.

concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The product of meromorphic functions is meromorphic and has a well-defined order.
concepts.c:locally-nonzero-function: A locally nonzero function has finite order, so orders add under multiplication.
concepts.c:pole-of-a-function: Each canonical factor contributes exactly one simple pole, which cancels one zero of $f$.
concepts.c:analytic-function: Order $0$ in normal form means $g$ is analytic and nonzero at the point.

source.note: mathlib takes g as toMeromorphicNFOn of (finprod of canonicalFactor R c ^ divisor f c) • f, and computes its divisor with divisor_smul and canonicalDecomposition_aux₂.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) with [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) $D$, circumradius $R$ and [inradius](c:inradius) $r$. The signed distances from $D$ to the three sides sum to $R+r$. A distance is negative exactly when the open segment from $D$ to the foot lies outside the triangle.

hypotheses.text: The points $A,B,C$ form a nondegenerate [triangle](c:triangle) with angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

conclusion: The signed distances $d_a,d_b,d_c$ from $D$ to $BC,CA,AB$ satisfy $d_a+d_b+d_c=R+r$.

proofs.name: Trigonometric identity
proofs.slogan: Write each signed distance as $R\cos$ of an angle, then compare the cosine sum with the inradius.
proofs.scope: All triangles, acute, right or obtuse. A right angle gives distance $0$, matching $\cos 90^\circ=0$.

roles.why: The triangle fixes the angles with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=180^\circ$, the circumcircle of radius $R$ and the incircle of radius $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that the signed distance from $D$ to $BC$ equals $R\cos\alpha$.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, so $M$ is the foot. For $\alpha<90^\circ$ the [inscribed angle](c:inscribed-angle) theorem gives $\angle BDC=2\alpha$ and $D$ on the side of $A$, so $DM=R\cos\alpha$. For $\alpha>90^\circ$ the point $D$ is across $BC$ and $DM=-R\cos\alpha$, which is the signed value. For $\alpha=90^\circ$, $D=M$.

steps.slogan: Show that the three cosines sum to $1+4\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$.
steps.detail: Since $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}=90^\circ-\frac{\gamma}{2}$, we get $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}$, and $\cos\gamma=1-2\sin^2\frac{\gamma}{2}$ with $\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}=\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$. The sum is $1+2\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big(\cos\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}-\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\big)$, and the bracket equals $2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}$.

The incircle touches $BC$ at $X$, and the tangent lengths are $BX=r\cot\frac{\beta}{2}$ and $XC=r\cot\frac{\gamma}{2}$. So $a=r\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}\big/\big(\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\big)$. The law of sines gives $a=2R\sin\alpha=4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}$. Equate the two values of $a$.

steps.slogan: Add the three distances and replace the cosine sum by the inradius formula.
steps.detail: By the first step, $d_a+d_b+d_c=R(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta+\cos\gamma)$. By the second step this is $R+4R\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}$. By the third step the last term is $r$, so the sum is $R+r$.

concepts.c:triangle: Its angles sum to $180^\circ$, which links the half-angles in the identities.
concepts.c:circumcenter: The circumcenter is the point whose distances to the sides are summed.
concepts.c:inradius: The inradius is the second term of the sum and has a half-angle formula.
concepts.c:inscribed-angle: It turns the angle at $A$ into the central angle $\angle BDC$.

source.note: Standard trigonometric proof through the half-angle formula for the inradius.
